content:
Looking around the landscape of limited space in Turing machines, I wanted to prove that constant-space TM accept exactly the regular languages. This essentially boils down to proving equivalence between one-way finite automata and two-way finite automata. A multi-tape TM without a work tape is essentially a two-way automaton.
Now my question: is there a plan to define 2-way finite automata in Cslib or does it make sense to define them on top of LTS like the others or should I just go ahead and prove it based on multi-tape TMs?

In order to prove that a language is regular, you need to show that it is accepted by a finite automaton (NA or DA), which contains an LTS or FLTS.
Reading your message again, I see that that is not what you were asking.

In the end, you need to make contact with an LTS or FLTS. Whether you go through 2-way finite automata is your choice. Currently I don't have any plan to work on 2-way finite automata, but I don't know if someone out there is working on it.
But LTS are inherently tied to reading the input from left to right, or could that be extended (I don’t know much about LTS)?
So my current plan is to show how to get a one way FA / LTS from a zero-tape TM that accepts the same language

Take a look at Kozen's textbook: https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4612-1844-9
Lectures 17 and 18 (page 119 onward) contain what you need. Its proof uses the Myhill-Nerode theorem, which is in CSLib: https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/blob/main/Cslib/Computability/Languages/MyhillNerode.lean
The text also refers to an alternative proof due to Vardi in an exercise.

Ah thanks! I was looking at the proof by shepherdson which also uses myhill nerode but the notation is a bit lacking. I wonder if myhill nerode is that useful in the end, at least in the proof by shepherdson you might as well construct the DFA directly, but maybe I also missed something.
What’s the difference between cslib‘s myhill-nerode and mathlib‘s?

I think CSLib's formulation Myhill-Nerode is more standard (in terms of textbooks) than Mathlib's and is basically the one in Wikipedia:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myhill–Nerode_theorem
Kozen’s writeup is perfect, thanks for the link! And indeed it also sound like Myhill-Nerode provides a benefit contrary to what Shepherdson’s writeup made me believe.

chris477 said:

But LTS are inherently tied to reading the input from left to right, or could that be extended (I don’t know much about LTS)?

Sidenote, perhaps now not relevant anymore:
I don't understand why LTS are inherently tied to anything.
AFAIK LTS typically get extended only when one needs to deal with certain kinds of non-discrete transition structures. LTSs are powerful enough to model most programming languages/computational models I know of, the exception being some specific probabilistic semantics (connected to the general aforementioned point), for which one then switches to even more general LTSs (kinda like going from FLTS to LTS).

I think the issue here is mainly technical. A 2-way finite automaton is essentially a Turing machine that has a read-only input tape and no working tapes. Its read pointer can go back and forth on the input tape before it decides to accept or reject. So it is not straightforward to show that it can be simulated by an NFA or DFA which can only read its input sequentially.

Ching-Tsun Chou said:

So it is not straightforward to show that it can be simulated by an NFA or DFA which can only read its input sequentially.

I think my statement is not exactly correct. What's proved is that the language accepted by any 2-way finite automaton is regular. That's different, and weaker, than the existence of a simulation of 2-way finite automaton by an NFA or DFA. I don't know if such a simulation exists, or even makes sense because the read pointer of the former can move back and forth.

Not sure I understand what you mean by „simulation“, but Myhill-Nerode is constructive and from the transition function of the two-way automaton we get a bound on the number of states, so the automaton can be derived from the proof.

By simulation I mean something like the notion developed in LTS/Simulation.lean, perhaps with some variations. The proof by Myhill-Nerode does produce a DFA, but I'm not sure that that DFA "simulates" the 2FA.
